metadata.title: LOR. — Open-source video meetings that remember
metadata.description: Meet, collaborate, and keep the useful record. LOR. is an Arabic-first open-source video meeting product.

brand.name: Live Open Rooms
brand.tagline: The room stays open. The thread stays useful.

control.title: Useful by default. Careful by design.

scope.title: Room-scoped evidence

faq.title: Questions before you join.
faq.intro: No marketing maze. These are the boundaries that shape the product today.

account.question: Do I need an account?
account.answer: No. Open a room link, type a display name, and join. The product home is intentionally a focused meeting entry point.

ai.question: Does the call need an AI key?
ai.answer: No. Video, audio, screen share, chat, board, notes, and local recording still work without an AI key or quota.

recording.question: What happens to a local recording?
recording.answer: The finished WebM stays in the same browser tab. LOR. does not upload, share, or retain it.

contribute.question: How can I contribute?
contribute.answer: Read CONTRIBUTING.md, choose a focused issue, run the checks, and open a small pull request. The repository keeps the workflow public.

hosting.question: Can I self-host today?
hosting.answer: Self-hosting is planned for v0.9. The hosted app is the current public path; follow the roadmap for the deployment contract.

final.eyebrow: Your next meeting can leave more behind
final.title: Make the meeting outcome easy to revisit.
final.body: Try the hosted app, then open the source when you want to see how it works or help shape what comes next.

metadata.title: LOR. Docs — Understand the room
metadata.description: A practical guide to running, understanding, and contributing to LOR. open-source video meetings.

docs.title: Everything you need to use and understand LOR.
docs.intro: Start a meeting, learn what happens to its results, and find the architecture and local setup when you want to contribute.

quickStart.title: Run the project locally.
quickStart.intro: Use the hosted app to try a meeting now. For code review or development, start with these commands and then add your local service settings.
quickStart.label: Quick start
quickStart.hint: Three commands, then add your local values
quickStart.note: Put LiveKit and Supabase values in .env.local. The call itself does not depend on an AI key.

what.title: A video room that keeps work in context.
what.body: Open a link, type a display name, and join. During the call, people can work together in the same room. Afterward, the useful record stays tied to its source instead of becoming a loose summary.
what.mixed: Arabic and English can share a sentence without asking the transcript to choose a different language.

workflow.title: From invitation to review.
workflow.intro: The flow is intentionally small. Each step has a clear owner and a clear edge.

join.title: Join
join.body: Share a room link, enter a name, and use the prejoin screen to check your devices before anyone hears you.

work.title: Work together
work.body: Keep chat, captions, a shared board, rich notes, and a local WebM close to the conversation.

review.title: Review and return
review.body: A host confirms decisions and participant-owned commitments. Timeline, Memory, and search return to retained evidence.

boundaries.title: Available now and planned later.
boundaries.intro: The product is deliberately explicit about what is shipped and what remains a contribution boundary.
boundaries.caption: Current and planned LOR. capabilities

call.label: Video meeting
call.today: LiveKit room, prejoin, chat, screen share
call.planned: No account system or paid tier

evidence.label: Retained evidence
evidence.today: Captions, decisions, tasks, Timeline, Memory, search

privacy.label: Privacy edges
privacy.today: Room scope, retention cleanup, local-only recording

extension.label: Extensions
extension.today: A focused repository and public issues
extension.planned: Integrations in v0.8; plugin ecosystem in v1.0

browser.title: Browser
browser.body: Displays the call and collaboration tools and holds encrypted user keys.

room.title: Live room
room.body: LiveKit carries media and shared state between participants.

record.title: Retained record
record.body: Postgres stores room-scoped transcripts and decisions under retention rules.

architecture.title: Three parts, clear boundaries.
architecture.intro: Media and shared meeting state travel over LiveKit. Next.js handles short request/response work; Postgres holds the retained projection.
architecture.note: The application does not run its own long-lived WebSocket server. That boundary keeps the same code usable on a hosted or future self-hosted box.

contribute.title: Start with a focused, testable issue.
contribute.body: Every contribution starts with a scoped issue, a branch, the required checks, and a pull request that explains what changed. Arabic RTL is the first layout pass; English LTR follows.

steps.choose: Choose a focused issue with acceptance criteria
steps.verify: Run typecheck, lint, tests, build, and the relevant browser check

help.title: Questions about use and data.
help.intro: If an answer is not here, the repository issue templates keep the next question concrete.

keys.question: Do API keys reach storage?
keys.answer: No. Operator keys stay server-only, and a participant's key is encrypted in the browser and forwarded without being written to the database, logs, or cache.

ai.question: Does an AI outage break the call?
ai.answer: No. AI features degrade to their bounded fallback; video, audio, collaboration, and local recording keep their own path.

selfHost.question: Can I self-host it now?
selfHost.answer: The self-hosting contract is planned for v0.9. The current public path is the hosted demo and the reproducible local development setup.

language.question: Why is Arabic the first pass?
language.answer: Mixed Arabic/English speech and RTL layout are first-class product constraints. Every UI change is checked in Arabic before English.

next.title: Choose your next depth
next.body: Try the room, read the project story, or open the source when you have a concrete question to answer.

keys.title: Getting a key
keys.intro: Captions send audio to a transcription service, and that costs somebody money. This server may offer a free allowance; when it runs out, or when there is none, you can use your own key instead. Here is where one comes from.
keys.freeYes: Yes — about {hours} hours of audio a day.
keys.freeNo: No free tier for the API. Pay as you go.
keys.limitsDetail: About {hoursPerHour} hours of audio an hour, and {requests} requests a minute.
keys.card_no: No — not to sign up and use the free tier.
keys.card_yes: Yes, before the API can be used.
keys.card_unstated: Their pricing page does not say.
keys.pathDirect: Straight from your browser to them. It never reaches this server, and neither does your key.
keys.pathProxy: Through this server, which forwards it and keeps nothing. Their API refuses requests made from a browser.
keys.howToAdd: To use one: turn captions on in a meeting, then open “Your own key” from the notice at the bottom of the screen. It is stored in your browser, encrypted, and you can remove it there at any time.
keys.noAffiliates: None of these are affiliate or referral links. Free tiers change — the date on each card is when its numbers were last read from the provider's own documentation.
keys.pathUntested: Through this server, which forwards it and keeps nothing. Nobody has tested whether they accept requests made directly from a browser, so LOR. takes the route that certainly works.
